stories.headline: Republicans hold lone Alaska House seat despite losing Senate, governor races
stories.note: Trump-endorsed Rep. Nick Begich held Alaska's only House seat despite a Democratic wave statewide.
body: Rep. Nick Begich, the Trump-endorsed Republican, has won another term in Alaska's at-large House seat. The race was called Wednesday night, more than two weeks after Election Day, once the state finished its ranked-choice tally.
Begich beat independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired teacher who had the Alaska Democratic Party's backing. Hill conceded and said he called Begich to congratulate him.

The win came against a tough backdrop. Democrat Mary Peltola unseated Sen. Dan Sullivan a day earlier, and Democrats also captured the governor's office for the first time in nearly 30 years. Nationally, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats and hold a 257-172 edge so far, with three races still uncalled.

The House race was also clouded by Eric Hafner, a self-described Democrat with no Alaska ties who is serving a federal prison sentence for threatening to kill judges and police. He took nearly 8% of the first-round vote. In the Senate race, the Justice Department opened a criminal probe after reports that Peltola's team helped recruit a same-named "Dan Sullivan" spoiler; Peltola denies any involvement.
Why it matters: In a bad midterm for the GOP, Begich's hold is one of the few bright spots, and the Peltola spoiler probe could keep raising questions about how Democrats won in Alaska.

stories.headline: Elected Somali daycare owner with fraud ties now revealed to also be married to illegal immigrant
stories.note: A newly elected Minnesota DFL lawmaker whose daycare is tied to a fraud-plagued program is married to an illegal immigrant, the Trump administration confirmed.
body: Abdi Daisane, a Minnesota DFL candidate who unseated a Republican to win House District 14A around St. Cloud, is married to a woman in the country illegally, a Trump administration official confirmed Wednesday after an Alpha News report.

His wife, Ayaan Aydid, 30, crossed the southern border in 2023 under the Biden administration. After the election, a BBC video resurfaced in which she described the crossing. "It wasn't a hard journey," she said.

Daisane runs Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud, which has taken in $7.29 million from Minnesota's Child Care Assistance Program since 2018 and nearly $600,000 in federal food-program money since 2020. Its sponsor for the food funds, Partners in Nutrition, recently paid an $18.5 million civil settlement over fraud.

When Fox News Digital visited the center after the election, it found tinted windows, a mostly empty lot and no children on the small playground. Daisane didn't respond to a request for comment. ICE posted that immigration laws apply to everyone "regardless of political status or power."
Why it matters: Minnesota's daycare and nutrition-program fraud scandals are already a major liability for Democrats there, and this case ties those concerns directly to illegal immigration.

stories.headline: Democrats could enter congressional majority in a government shutdown
stories.note: Republicans warn the new Democratic majority could open with a shutdown fight over Iran war funding ahead of the Dec. 11 deadline.
body: With federal funding set to run out Dec. 11, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they worry Democrats, emboldened by their midterm wins, will make highly partisan demands that could trigger another government shutdown.
Rep. Mike Haridopolos of Florida said he fears Democrats will return to what he called their "winning playbook" of shutting down the government. Rep. Ryan Zinke of Montana also said he is concerned.

Congress pushed the fight past the election with a stopgap that keeps 2026 spending levels running through Dec. 11. Most lawmakers expect another short-term extension, though how long it should last is still in dispute.

Democrats blame Senate Republicans for the holdup. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on House Appropriations, wants a stopgap only through March and signaled Democrats won't fund "a war of choice" in Iran. Sens. Warren, Duckworth and Gillibrand are pushing an amendment to restrict war funding, which Schumer challenger Chris Van Hollen supports. Sen. Kevin Cramer warned that move is "playing with fire."
Why it matters: If Democrats tie government funding to limits on the Iran war, Republicans can argue they are putting troops at risk before the new majority is even sworn in.

stories.headline: DHS denounces TX officials for allegedly planning to end cooperation with ICE
stories.note: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned newly elected Texas Democrats that ending ICE cooperation would be a dereliction of duty.
body: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is pushing back on Texas Democrats who plan to end or limit local cooperation with ICE after the party swept statewide offices on Nov. 3.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire issued a Nov. 6 order barring city police from notifying ICE about illegal immigrants they encounter in nonviolent situations. The mayors of Austin and San Antonio quickly followed with orders limiting police cooperation.

Mullin told Fox that Texas becoming a sanctuary state would be "one of the worst derelictions of duty" in a long time. He urged Governor-elect Hinojosa and other leaders to keep working with DHS, noting that 7 of the 10 safest U.S. cities cooperate with ICE.

DHS pointed to Texas cases it says show what is at stake. They include two Venezuelan nationals sentenced in a San Antonio child-trafficking case, an MS-13-linked Honduran deported after repeated arrests, and an Afghan woman in Fort Worth who admitted to an ISIS-inspired Election Day shooting plot and was removed in September.
Why it matters: Sanctuary policies in a border state give Republicans a clear public-safety contrast with Texas's new Democratic leadership right from the start.

stories.headline: Florida eyes poaching NYPD officers after Mamdani dismantles elite unit
stories.note: Florida Republicans are recruiting NYPD officers after Mayor Mamdani disbanded the elite Strategic Response Group, and even some NYC Democrats object.
body: Florida Republicans are inviting NYPD officers to head south after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Councilman Chi Ossé announced they will disband the department's Strategic Response Group (SRG).

"Florida is always looking for well-qualified new officers," said Sen. Ashley Moody, the state's former attorney general. Miami-Dade Commissioner Roberto Gonzalez told NYPD officers, "We're hiring." Earlier, Volusia County Sheriff Michael Chitwood ran recruiting billboards in Times Square.

Mamdani is replacing the SRG with a new Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, staffed by unarmed civilians without arrest powers who can call in uniformed police if needed. Mamdani and Ossé say protest response and counterterrorism should be handled separately.

Critics include fellow Democrat James Gennaro, a Queens councilman, who said the change raises doubts about the city's ability to handle major incidents, including active-shooter attacks. Former Commissioner Bill Bratton, who created the 600-officer unit, warned that the city can't reorganize away the threats it was built to meet.
Why it matters: Florida is using Mamdani's policing cuts to sell itself as the pro-police alternative, and the criticism from Democrats in his own city shows how divisive the move is.

stories.headline: Jeffries brushes off opposition from far-left Dems who voted no: 'We're going to work together'
stories.note: Eleven Democrats opposed Jeffries' speaker nomination, with far-left members demanding he back abolishing ICE and Medicare-for-all.
body: House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker on Wednesday, but 11 Democrats voted against him, a group made up largely of incoming far-left members.

Those opponents, including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez, said talks with Jeffries are "ongoing." They say voters gave them a mandate on Medicare-for-all, "stopping ICE terror," getting money out of politics and Gaza.

Jeffries wouldn't say whether he will take up demands such as abolishing ICE or ending military aid to Israel. He said the 260-member majority would "work together" and focus on fighting "MAGA extremism, not each other."
Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III, who is succeeding Rep. Jasmine Crockett, missed the vote because of illness, but his office said he would have voted no.
Why it matters: Before the new majority is even sworn in, Jeffries faces a left wing that wants to abolish ICE, which gives Republicans a ready-made line of attack.

stories.headline: 'You will regret it': Angry resident confronts Democratic mayor during chaotic council meeting
stories.note: Immigration activists in Sacramento threatened Democratic Mayor Kevin McCarty and forced the council's fifth recess of the year.
body: A Sacramento City Council meeting broke down Tuesday when a woman, whom The Sacramento Bee identified as a local immigration activist, threatened Democratic Mayor Kevin McCarty's career during public comment and tried to read out his home address.

"If you do not vote in our interest again, you will regret it," she told the mayor, warning that protesters would shut things down. Officials cut her microphone as she started reciting the address and called a recess. The council returned about 20 minutes later, and no one was removed.
Earlier in the meeting, McCarty had postponed a vote on a $3.7 million Department of Homeland Security grant because of questions about data-sharing provisions.

The Bee reported it was the fifth time this year the council has recessed because of disruptions, mostly from activists angry about immigration enforcement and the city's sanctuary policies. McCarty's office declined to comment.
Why it matters: Even in a deep-blue capital that already has sanctuary policies, far-left activists are turning on Democratic leaders, a sign of the party's internal fight over immigration.
